concepts.title: Select repeated groups
concepts.text: After sort makes equal IDs neighbors, uniq -d prints each group with two or more members once. uniq alone also prints singletons; sort -u removes the evidence of repetition. The small example finds repeated IDs without writing a report.

concepts.title: Validate before changing the result
concepts.text: A failed job should not destroy the last useful report. Checking only the first source is insufficient: a later source could be missing. Finish the complete check before opening the destination with >.

concepts.title: Separate checking from writing
concepts.text: A helper can inspect all source arguments and return a status without changing files. The caller either reports a problem or builds the result. The example performs only the check, with different filenames.

concepts.title: Plan the replacement and append phases

after.title: Combine the file and filename checks
after.text: A && B runs B only when A succeeds with status 0. In the example, [ -f "$item" ] first checks that the selected name is a real virtual file; [ "$item" = "$target" ] then tests whether its text exactly equals the destination name. Both checks must succeed to reject a collision. The = inside [ ] compares two values; target=practice.txt outside [ ] assigns a value.

original_teaching.example:
build_list() {
    for item in "$@"; do
        if [ -f "$item" ] && [ "$item" = "$target" ]; then
            printf 'Choose a separate list file\n' >&2
            return 2
        fi
    done
    printf 'Notes\n' > "$target"
    for item in "$@"; do
        if [ -f "$item" ]; then
            printf '%s\n' "$item" >> "$target"
        fi
    done
}
target=practice.txt
build_list *.note

after.title: Recognize the test command spelling
after.text: test -z "$2" is the same empty-text check as [ -z "$2" ]. With test, omit the closing ]; the options and success statuses are the same. test "$#" -ne 2 checks whether the supplied argument count differs from two. As in earlier guards, A || B tries B only after A fails, so either invalid check can select the error branch. The example uses this spelling before its new case decision.

concepts.title: Choose the first matching arm
concepts.text: case "$1" in starts a decision using the entire first argument. A pattern ends at ), its commands follow, and ;; finishes that arm. The first match wins; later arms do not run. End the decision with esac. Patterns separated by | choose the same commands, such as quick|summary).

concepts.title: An explicit default is part of the interface
concepts.text: Use *) as the final arm for everything else. Print a useful diagnostic to standard error and choose a nonzero exit status. Check help separately before ordinary argument counts when help has a different interface. No-match alone returns 0; it is not an error handler.

concepts.title: Patterns and values have different roles
concepts.text: The selector stays one value, even if it contains spaces or wildcard-looking text. In patterns, unquoted * matches any number of bytes and ? one byte; quoting either makes it literal. quick* is a broad pattern; 'quick*' expects a literal star. Use exact mode names here. When printing a label, quote it and use a fixed printf format.

concepts.title: Keep the workbench boundary clear
concepts.text: Patterns here support simple * and ? with C/POSIX byte matching. A byte is not necessarily a whole UTF8 character. Bracket patterns such as [ab] and fallthrough operators ;& and ;;& are outside this workbench; use ;;. These limits do not restrict quoted literal text.

after.title: A printf format can repeat for several values
after.text: printf 'Original: <%s>\n' "${original[@]}" receives one separate value per array entry. printf repeats its format while values remain, so each entry gets its own labeled line. With no value arguments, printf still uses the format once with an empty %s; use a for loop when an empty array must print no rows. Both example arrays are nonempty.

concepts.title: A copy stays available
concepts.text: original=("${stops[@]}") copies every current value, including empty entries. Later changes to stops leave original intact. Each entry is copied separately, so changing one list does not change the other.

concepts.title: One entry differs from the whole list
concepts.text: For an existing Bash indexed array, stops='Workshop' changes entry 0 and keeps later entries. stops=('Workshop') replaces the entire list with one entry. An ordinary $stops read also reads entry 0; it does not mean every entry.

concepts.title: Investigate the lost work
concepts.text: The example creates both lists itself. In the assignment only REPLACEMENT and the arguments are supplied. The starter already records an original copy; run it and find why jobs disappear. One empty job is still a job, so test the count rather than whether its first text is empty.

printf 'Updated: <%s>\n' "${stops[@]}"
